Efficacy and safety of a targeted-release formulation of
budesonide in patients with primary IgA nephropathy
(NefIgArd): 2-year results from a randomised phase 3 trial
Richard Lafayette, Jens Kristensen, Andrew Stone, Jürgen Floege, Vladimir Tesař, Hernán Trimarchi, Hong Zhang, Necmi Eren, Alexander Paliege,
Heather N Reich, Brad H Rovin, Jonathan Barratt, on behalf of the NefIgArd trial investigators
Summary
Background IgA nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated kidney disease and a major cause of kidney failure
worldwide. The gut mucosal immune system is implicated in its pathogenesis, and Nefecon is a novel, oral,
targeted-release formulation of budesonide designed to act at the gut mucosal level. We present findings from the
2-year, phase 3 NefIgArd trial of Nefecon in patients with IgA nephropathy.
Methods In this phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adult patients (aged
≥18 years) with primary IgA nephropathy, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 35-90 mL/min per 1·73 m2,
and persistent proteinuria (urine protein-creatinine ratio ≥0·8 g/g or proteinuria ≥1 g/24 h) despite optimised renin-
angiotensin system blockade were enrolled at 132 hospital-based clinical sites in 20 countries worldwide. Patients
were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 16 mg/day oral capsules of Nefecon or matching placebo for 9 months,
followed by a 15-month observational follow-up period off study drug. Randomisation via an interactive response
technology system was stratified according to baseline proteinuria (<2 or ≥2 g/24 h), baseline eGFR (<60 or ≥60 mL/min
per 1·73 m2), and region (Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, or South America). Patients, investigators, and site
staff were masked to treatment assignment throughout the 2-year trial. Optimised supportive care was also continued
throughout the trial. The primary efficacy endpoint was time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years. Efficacy and
safety analyses were done in the full analysis set (ie, all randomly assigned patients). The trial was registered on
ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03643965, and is completed.
Findings Patients were recruited to the NefIgArd trial between Sept 5, 2018, and Jan 20, 2021, with 364 patients (182 per
treatment group) randomly assigned in the full analysis set. 240 (66%) patients were men and 124 (34%) were women,
and 275 (76%) identified as White. The time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years showed a statistically significant
treatment benefit with Nefecon versus placebo (difference 5·05 mL/min per 1·73 m2 [95% CI 3·24 to 7·38], p<0·0001),
with a time-weighted average change of -2·47 mL/min per 1·73 m2 (95% CI -3·88 to -1·02) reported with Nefecon
and -7·52 mL/min per 1·73 m2 (-8·83 to -6·18) reported with placebo. The most commonly reported treatment-
emergent adverse events during treatment with Nefecon were peripheral oedema (31 [17%] patients, vs placebo,
seven [4%] patients), hypertension (22 [12%] vs six [3%]), muscle spasms (22 [12%] vs seven [4%]), acne (20 [11%] vs
two [1%]), and headache (19 [10%] vs 14 [8%]). No treatment-related deaths were reported.
Interpretation A 9-month treatment period with Nefecon provided a clinically relevant reduction in eGFR decline and
a durable reduction in proteinuria versus placebo, providing support for a disease-modifying effect in patients with
IgA nephropathy. Nefecon was also well tolerated, with a safety profile as expected for a locally acting oral budesonide
product.

Efficacy and safety data were analysed in the full analysis
set, which included all randomly assigned patients (apart
from two patients who were prospectively excluded due to
being incorrectly randomised, and patients recruited for
regulatory requirements in China after enrolment of the
planned 360 patients was complete).
The primary aim of the efficacy analysis was to describe
the efficacy of the 9-month regimen of Nefecon 16 mg/day
in comparison with placebo, free from the effects of rescue
medication and irrespective of any early discontinuation of
study treatment. The reasons for exclusion from the
primary efficacy analyses of data impacted by rescue
medication or prohibited immunosuppressive medications
for non-IgA nephropathy indications are described in the
appendix (p 3).
For the primary efficacy endpoint (time-weighted
average of eGFR over 2 years), each timepoint was
weighted in proportion to the time elapsed since the
previous recording. Therefore, recordings made at
18 and 24 months received twice as much weight as those
made at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. The weights totalled 1 so
that the treatment effect could be interpreted as the
average effect over 2 years. Data were log-transformed
before analysis and data included at baseline and
24 months were the log of the geometric mean of the two
replicate values recorded at each timepoint, respectively.
Missing data were imputed by multiple imputation
before calculation of each patient's time-weighted
average, conditional on their previous eGFR measure
ments. Log-transformed time-weighted average values in
each imputed dataset were analysed with use of robust
regression with log-baseline eGFR fitted as a covariate.
Results were combined across imputations according to
Rubin's rules.21 Pre-specified sensitivity analyses were
done that varied missing data assumptions and that
analysed data with a mixed model repeated measures
approach. In pre-specified supplementary analyses, the
primary analysis was repeated in the per-protocol
population (all patients in the full analysis set for whom
no major protocol deviations occurred during the study
period), and in the full analysis set including data
recorded after the use of rescue medication or other
prohibited immunosuppressive medications. A post-hoc
analysis was also done that excluded data observed after
starting SGLT2 inhibitors after baseline (appendix p 6).

answers.justification: The supplement reports the prespecified alternative-missing-data-assumption analysis, in which incomplete follow-up among early treatment discontinuers was imputed using treatment duration and post-12-month UPCR information before rescue. Its treatment estimate (5.14; 95% CI 3.24 to 7.58) was close to the primary estimate (5.05; 3.24 to 7.38). 50|1.4.1. Definition of rescue medication
51|Rescue medication was defined as any immunosuppressive medication that would be expected to materially
52|impact efficacy, regardless of whether the medication was used for IgAN. A blinded medical review of
53|concomitant therapy was performed to document which patients were defined as having rescue medication for
54|IgAN or prohibited immunosuppressive medications for non-IgAN indications, and therefore had some or all of
55|their data excluded from the relevant efficacy analyses. When the dose and duration of treatment received was
56|considered unlikely to have impacted all subsequent data, only data at specified visits were excluded. Initiation
57|of dialysis, renal transplantation, and renal-related death (although the latter did not occur) were also included
58|with rescue medication as reasons for exclusion of impacted data from the primary efficacy analyses.

61|Time-weighted average of eGFR measurements over 2 years were analysed using robust regression, having
62|multiply imputed any missing data first in three phases: an imputation, analysis, and pooling phase. Robust
63|regression was selected because previous eGFR data contained a small sub-population of patients having
64|extreme outlying data resulting from very rapid progression of disease. Robust regression avoids results being
65|unduly influenced by a small subset of patients with outlying data. Data at each individual time point were
66|log-transformed prior to analysis.

68|The first step of the imputation phase was to create data with a monotone data structure across time points
69|having imputed 20 datasets separately within each treatment arm. The number of burn-in iterations was set to
70|200, and observations were sampled every 200 iterations within the same chain for each imputed dataset. In the
71|second step of the imputation phase, data at each timepoint were multiply imputed using a regression method

4|in the first step. Having imputed any missing data, the time weighted average over 2 years was calculated for

7|In the analysis phase, time weighted average eGFR data were analysed using robust regression with independent
8|variables of treatment and log-transformed baseline eGFR. M-estimation was used with Huber weights and a
9|cut-off value of 2, with the median method used to estimate the scale parameter. This approach means that
10|standardised residuals with an absolute value of ≤2, corresponding to the central 95% of the data if normally
11|distributed, have equal weight, and outlying data are weighted according to a pre-specified function, Wc(x),
12|which gives lower weights to the most outlying data where Wc(x)=min{1,c|x|} and x is the standardised
13|residual, corresponding to least square standardised residuals in the first iteration. Given that dependent variables
14|are categorical and inclusion criteria for the only continuous covariate, log-transformed baseline eGFR, prevents
15|this variable from having outlying values, M-estimation was deemed appropriate.
16|
17|In the pooling phase, estimated treatment effects and associated standard errors from each imputation were
18|combined using Rubin's rules to provide an overall treatment effect, associated 95% confidence interval (CI),
19|and one-sided p value. For the purposes of presentation, data were back transformed and expressed as the mean
20|change from baseline in eGFR averaged over 2 years in each treatment arm and derived directly from the robust
21|regression analysis performed on the log scale by multiplying the baseline geometric mean eGFR, pooled across
22|treatment arms, with the ratio of geometric least-squares (LS) means within each arm minus 1. Diagnostic plots
23|for the analysis models and the residuals were checked. No evidence of violation of the modelling assumptions
24|was observed.

27|The primary supportive analysis of 2-year eGFR total slope using a random coefficients analysis was planned
28|prior to unblinding Part A. However, in the presence of an acute effect this analysis method does not provide an
29|accurate estimate of the difference in the eGFR decline over 2 years as slope is not forced through baseline and,
30|as a result, it underestimates the magnitude of the treatment effect between the targeted-release formulation of
31|budesonide (Nefecon; Tarpeyo/Kinpeygo [Calliditas Therapeutics, Stockholm, Sweden]) and placebo.

33|Therefore, 2-year eGFR total slope was estimated as half of the between-arm difference in mean change from
34|baseline to 2 years derived from a robust regression analysis of the multiply imputed values of log-transformed
35|eGFR at 2 years used in the primary endpoint calculation. An analysis of 2-year eGFR total slope using a linear
36|spline mixed-effects analysis,7 with a fixed knot at 3 months, was also pre-specified prior to unblinding the full
37|study to provide a more accurate estimate of the magnitude of the 2-year eGFR total slope. This analysis method
38|was used in a previous meta-analysis by Inker et al.8

9|Summary
10|Background IgA nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated kidney disease and a major cause of kidney failure
11|worldwide. The gut mucosal immune system is implicated in its pathogenesis, and Nefecon is a novel, oral,
12|targeted-release formulation of budesonide designed to act at the gut mucosal level. We present findings from the
13|2-year, phase 3 NefIgArd trial of Nefecon in patients with IgA nephropathy.
14|Methods In this phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adult patients (aged
15|≥18 years) with primary IgA nephropathy, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 35-90 mL/min per 1·73 m2,
16|and persistent proteinuria (urine protein-creatinine ratio ≥0·8 g/g or proteinuria ≥1 g/24 h) despite optimised renin-
17|angiotensin system blockade were enrolled at 132 hospital-based clinical sites in 20 countries worldwide. Patients
18|were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 16 mg/day oral capsules of Nefecon or matching placebo for 9 months,
19|followed by a 15-month observational follow-up period off study drug. Randomisation via an interactive response
20|technology system was stratified according to baseline proteinuria (<2 or ≥2 g/24 h), baseline eGFR (<60 or ≥60 mL/min
21|per 1·73 m2), and region (Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, or South America). Patients, investigators, and site
22|staff were masked to treatment assignment throughout the 2-year trial. Optimised supportive care was also continued
23|throughout the trial. The primary efficacy endpoint was time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years. Efficacy and
24|safety analyses were done in the full analysis set (ie, all randomly assigned patients). The trial was registered on
25|ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03643965, and is completed.
26|Findings Patients were recruited to the NefIgArd trial between Sept 5, 2018, and Jan 20, 2021, with 364 patients (182 per
27|treatment group) randomly assigned in the full analysis set. 240 (66%) patients were men and 124 (34%) were women,
28|and 275 (76%) identified as White. The time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years showed a statistically significant
29|treatment benefit with Nefecon versus placebo (difference 5·05 mL/min per 1·73 m2 [95% CI 3·24 to 7·38], p<0·0001),
30|with a time-weighted average change of -2·47 mL/min per 1·73 m2 (95% CI -3·88 to -1·02) reported with Nefecon
31|and -7·52 mL/min per 1·73 m2 (-8·83 to -6·18) reported with placebo. The most commonly reported treatment-
32|emergent adverse events during treatment with Nefecon were peripheral oedema (31 [17%] patients, vs placebo,
33|seven [4%] patients), hypertension (22 [12%] vs six [3%]), muscle spasms (22 [12%] vs seven [4%]), acne (20 [11%] vs
34|two [1%]), and headache (19 [10%] vs 14 [8%]). No treatment-related deaths were reported.
35|Interpretation A 9-month treatment period with Nefecon provided a clinically relevant reduction in eGFR decline and
36|a durable reduction in proteinuria versus placebo, providing support for a disease-modifying effect in patients with
37|IgA nephropathy. Nefecon was also well tolerated, with a safety profile as expected for a locally acting oral budesonide
38|product.

73|Research in context
74|Evidence before this study
75|The present phase 3 NefIgArd trial was designed and initiated
76|following the findings of the earlier phase 2b NEFIGAN trial by
77|Fellström and colleagues (2017), which reported reduced
78|proteinuria and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
79|treatment benefit favouring Nefecon, a novel, oral,
80|targeted-release capsule formulation of budesonide specifically
81|developed for the treatment of IgAN, versus placebo in
82|patients with IgA nephropathy. All evidence considered before
83|initiating the original phase 2b NEFIGAN trial is described
84|therein. IgA nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated
85|kidney disease and is a major cause of kidney failure. No
86|effective disease-modifying strategies are available for IgA
87|nephropathy, with treatment recommendations focusing on
88|providing optimised supportive care (including maximally
89|tolerated renin-angiotensin system blockade). Systemic
90|glucocorticoids have been tested in patients with IgA
91|nephropathy, but recent studies (the STOP-IgAN and TESTING
92|trials) have reported mixed efficacy outcomes and increased
93|risk of serious adverse events and of severe infections with
94|their use. A growing body of evidence supports the role of the
95|gut mucosal immune system and mucosal-derived
96|galactose-deficient IgA1 (gd-IgA1) in the pathogenesis of
97|primary IgA nephropathy, with Peyer's patches in the gut
98|identified as a major source of gd-IgA1. Nefecon, developed by
99|Calliditas Therapeutics, is designed to act locally in the distal
100|ileum, where the Peyer's patches are highly concentrated.
101|Separate meta-analyses have shown that reduction in
102|proteinuria and slowing of eGFR decline were predictive of
103|treatment effects on long-term kidney outcomes in chronic
104|kidney disease, including IgA nephropathy. Thus, these markers
105|were used as surrogate endpoints for demonstrating clinical
106|benefit in the phase 3 NefIgArd trial of Nefecon.
107|Added value of this study
108|This full 2-year trial provides evidence that 9 months of
109|treatment with Nefecon 16 mg/day, led to a significant
110|reduction in the average decline in eGFR over 2 years in patients
111|with primary IgA nephropathy, which was preserved during a
112|15-month follow-up period off drug. In addition, a durable
113|reduction in proteinuria was observed for the entire period.
114|Importantly, for the early management of patients with
115|primary IgA nephropathy to delay disease progression, this
116|positive effect of Nefecon on eGFR was independent of baseline
117|proteinuria, and resulted in an approximate 50% reduction in
118|the decline of eGFR compared with placebo over
119|the 2-year period. Nefecon was shown to be well tolerated and
120|had a safety profile that reflected a locally, rather than
121|systemically, acting glucocorticoid product.
122|Implications of all the available evidence
123|Combined with what is known already in the field, the full
124|2-year NefIgArd trial findings provide support to the strategy of
125|targeting the gut-kidney axis in IgA nephropathy. The present
126|results also indicate that treatment with Nefecon 16 mg/day
127|can modify the disease course of IgA nephropathy in a clinically
128|meaningful way and with minimally increased risk of serious
129|adverse events when compared with placebo treatment.

49|Statistical analysis
50|Further details on the statistical analysis methods are
51|included in the appendix (pp 3-5). With 360 patients, the
52|study had 90% power to detect a statistically significant
53|difference in eGFR at 2 years, with use of a one-sided
54|alpha of 2·5%, assuming a difference in mean eGFR of
55|2·24 mL/min per 1·73 m2 at 2 years.17 An endpoint
56|hierarchy was defined to provide control of the type I
57|error rate of 2·5%, one-sided across key endpoints of the
58|study. All p values presented are one-sided, apart from
59|interaction test p values, which are two-sided.
60|Efficacy and safety data were analysed in the full analysis
61|set, which included all randomly assigned patients (apart
62|from two patients who were prospectively excluded due to
63|being incorrectly randomised, and patients recruited for
64|regulatory requirements in China after enrolment of the
65|planned 360 patients was complete).
66|The primary aim of the efficacy analysis was to describe
67|the efficacy of the 9-month regimen of Nefecon 16 mg/day
68|in comparison with placebo, free from the effects of rescue
69|medication and irrespective of any early discontinuation of
70|study treatment. The reasons for exclusion from the
71|primary efficacy analyses of data impacted by rescue
72|medication or prohibited immunosuppressive medications
73|for non-IgA nephropathy indications are described in the
74|appendix (p 3).
75|For the primary efficacy endpoint (time-weighted
76|average of eGFR over 2 years), each timepoint was
77|weighted in proportion to the time elapsed since the
78|previous recording. Therefore, recordings made at
79|18 and 24 months received twice as much weight as those
80|made at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. The weights totalled 1 so
81|that the treatment effect could be interpreted as the
82|average effect over 2 years. Data were log-transformed
83|before analysis and data included at baseline and
84|24 months were the log of the geometric mean of the two
85|replicate values recorded at each timepoint, respectively.

87|before calculation of each patient's time-weighted
88|average, conditional on their previous eGFR measure
89|ments. Log-transformed time-weighted average values in
90|each imputed dataset were analysed with use of robust
91|regression with log-baseline eGFR fitted as a covariate.
92|Results were combined across imputations according to
93|Rubin's rules.21 Pre-specified sensitivity analyses were
94|done that varied missing data assumptions and that
95|analysed data with a mixed model repeated measures
96|approach. In pre-specified supplementary analyses, the
97|primary analysis was repeated in the per-protocol
98|population (all patients in the full analysis set for whom
99|no major protocol deviations occurred during the study

101|recorded after the use of rescue medication or other

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When exact extent cannot be determined directly, weigh outcome-specific follow-up accounting and other source-supported information for a probably yes or probably no judgment. If the extent remains unknown because that evidence does not support a reasonable inference, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement. Outcome-specific observed/expected follow-up time can inform a probable judgment, but is not a participant-observation fraction; vital status alone does not ascertain nonfatal components. Explain what the evidence implies about missing outcomes for the approved estimate.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when neither direct nor indirect evidence supports a reasonable judgment about availability after bounded retrieval. Imprecise quantification alone does not require no_information. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.

questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Weigh evidence for and against likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances, including comparable outcome follow-up and continued ascertainment after treatment stopping. Such contextual counterevidence is not proof of non-informative censoring; absence of precise reasons or timing alone does not require no_information, and absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.

Full guidance section 6.1, p. 39 distinguishes genuinely missing measurements (D3) from available outcomes deliberately excluded from analysis (D2). paired_examples.changed_premise: whether the approved outcome was actually ascertained
left_facts: The outcome was ascertained for every randomized participant at the approved window.
right_facts: The report gives an analysis denominator but does not establish outcome ascertainment.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Keep observed outcome availability separate from analysis membership and preserve No information when extent is unresolved.

left_facts: Administrative censoring occurred at a common cutoff after the approved window.
right_facts: Participants stopped follow-up after worsening symptoms before the approved window.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Separate administrative censoring from a mechanism that could depend on the true outcome.

paired_examples.changed_premise: whether the examined assumptions address the documented missingness mechanism
left_facts: Post-hoc sensitivity analyses estimate the same approved Result.
Their estimates remain close to the primary estimate.
Changed assumptions address the documented reasons for missing outcomes; retained assumptions are supported by relevant observed information.
right_facts: Post-hoc sensitivity analyses estimate the same approved Result.
Their estimates remain close to the primary estimate.
The analyses retain a missingness assumption whose plausibility for the documented reasons for missing outcomes remains unresolved.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Compare changed and retained assumptions with the documented mechanism. Numerical agreement is reassurance within those assumptions; post-hoc timing alone does not invalidate D3 evidence, and an explicit MNAR analysis is not universally required. Keep unresolved plausibility distinct from evidence that bias occurred.

paired_examples.changed_premise: strength of evidence that missingness depends on the true outcome
left_facts: The reported reason for loss could be related to the unobserved outcome, but the link is unresolved.
right_facts: Source records show that worsening outcome status commonly preceded and explained follow-up loss.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Keep a plausible pathway distinct from evidence that makes dependence likely; neither follows from missing counts alone.

paired_examples.changed_premise: whether outcome follow-up continued after treatment stopped
left_facts: Twelve participants stopped assigned treatment after documented worsening.
The approved endpoint was due at day 90 for all randomized participants.
All 12 participants were assessed at day 90 after stopping treatment.
right_facts: Twelve participants stopped assigned treatment after documented worsening.
The approved endpoint was due at day 90 for all randomized participants.
Outcome follow-up ended before day 90 for all 12 participants after they stopped treatment.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Treatment discontinuation alone does not establish missing outcomes. Check follow-up and the possible effect of unavailable outcomes.
